report_excerpt: For cost Proof1.1, even the existing initialization's full checks at each of <=n stages stay cubic; an early initialization invariant/range failure only shortens that path. n<=2 has no such stage or below-first-subdiagonal position. Proof1.2 uses bounded-support factors; forming the few polynomial-vector components costs at most O(r) for interval lengthr (even a full dot over that interval), within O(nr). Identity copying and symbolic product factors fit the same bounds. Row-major direct interval enumeration includes all potentially changed below-band entries and excludes no possible violation, including a target overwrite. Complement-zero induction is independent of shift selection and rounding accuracy. The original persistent2x2 example therefore still reaches the same finite status if its arithmetic admits those identities, but its scan work is now quadratic per pass. No benchmark or convergence experiment was run.

proof_steps.claim: Hessenberg reduction uses at most $\max(n-2,0)$ reflector steps. For $n\ge3$, forming one reflector costs $O(n)$ scalar operations, and applying its two-sided similarity to the remaining dense submatrix costs $O(n^2)$; summing over at most $n$ steps gives $O(n^3)$. Any full initialization zero-pattern checks also cost at most $O(n^2)$ per stage, hence at most $O(n^3)$ in total. For $n=1,2$, there are no such reflector stages and no below-subdiagonal entries.

For an active block of size $r\ge2$, a Francis sweep has at most $\max(r-2,0)+1$ initial/chase reflectors of length two or three. Each acts on a bounded number of rows and columns across at most $n$ entries. For a processed interval $[a,b]$ of length $r$, every matrix write has a row or column in that interval. Before the chase, initialization or the preceding accepted check has established that the complementary below-subdiagonal positions are zero. The prescribed post-block check enumerates only the positions touching this interval: at most $nr$ in its rows and $nr$ in its columns, plus the $n$ row-loop visits. It is therefore equivalent to the full Hessenberg check and costs $O(nr)$, since every active interval has $r\ge2$. The disjoint active lengths sum to at most $n$, so all these checks cost $O(n^2)$ per sweep, even if every polynomial vector is zero and all factors are identities. The explicit partition/deflation passes and direct shift-table lookups also fit within $O(n^2)$; for $n=1$ there is no active sweep. Thus a full sweep, including all non-controller status work, costs $O(n^2)$. The linear sweep budgets therefore give $O(n^3)$ matrix work for the two Schur calls. A range, breakdown, invariant, budget, missing-shift or unavailable-sign failure stops within these bounded loops and adds only its partial-output work; it cannot increase their worst-case count. The same bound covers materializing the recorded factor products: initialization contributes $O(n^3)$ and each bounded-support chase factor updates only a bounded number of dense-factor columns, at cost $O(n)$.

Each exact Schur-certificate matrix product, the transform $U^*CV$, and the final transform $UYV^*$ cost $O(n^3)$. The block substitution has at most $n^2$ block pairs; each pair sums at most $O(n)$ earlier blocks of bounded size and solves a system of dimension at most four, so all substitution work is $O(n^3)$.

Each sweep checks at most $O(n)$ active blocks, and initialization and final checks add at most $O(n)$ such calls. With $O(n)$ sweeps there are at most $O(n^2)$ sign/representation-controller calls. A bounded call executes at most $K$ instructions, giving $O(Kn^2)$ work; the fixed built-in exact polynomial tree and rational/dyadic recipe are constant-size special cases. In arbitrary-terminating mode their actual total work is precisely the additional $C_{\rm aux}$.

The backward-error accumulator starts with one outward Frobenius norm of the input, costing $O(n^2)$ by the declared entrywise evaluator model. Each similarity uses a fixed number of scalar upper-bound calls once its local coefficient is evaluated. The explicit real/complex coefficient formulas require $O(m)$ scalar operations on active dimension $m$: their dimension-dependent powers can be formed by repeated multiplication and a square root for a half-integer exponent. Thus the at most $n$ initialization coefficients cost $O(n^2)$ in total, while each length-two/three chase coefficient costs $O(1)$. There are $O(n^2)$ chase similarities over the linear number of sweeps. Each recorded one-entry deflation has Frobenius norm equal to the modulus of its signed stored value, evaluated from that one-entry list with $O(1)$ scalar work; at most $O(n)$ such writes occur per sweep, hence $O(n^2)$ in total. Each stage then makes a fixed number of recurrence calls. Unavailable coefficient/evaluator results only stop certificate bookkeeping. Consequently this entire ancillary accumulation costs $O(n^2)$ and fits inside the cubic matrix-work bound, including failure branches.

The reductions, sweeps, exact certificates, transforms, block sums and fixed-size solves contribute $O(n^3)$, and step 1.4 supplies the complete control contribution. Adding them gives $O(n^3+Kn^2)$ and the fixed-$K$ cubic consequence, or $O(n^3+C_{\rm aux})$ for the richer terminating route. No bound on integer bit length or bit-operation cost is used.
